source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 17% of people in Netherlands were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
17.3% of health spending in Netherlands was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
0.6% of people in Netherlands reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
6% of hospital care costs in Netherlands were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
21% of outpatient medical care costs in Netherlands were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
67% of dental care costs in Netherlands were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
32% of pharmaceutical costs in Netherlands were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

A few countries (such as the Netherlands and Switzerland) have achieved universality through compulsory private health insurance – supported by public subsidies and strong regulation on the scope and depth of coverage.
Israel and the Netherlands had the largest supplementary health insurance market (over 80% of the population).

However, over 8% of the population reported unmet care needs in Latvia (8.4%), Estonia (8.5%), Finland (8.6%), Canada (9.1%) and Greece (12.1%), while in Germany, the Netherlands and Czechia, fewer than 1% of the population reported unmet needs for medical care.
More than 8% of people in Greece, Latvia and Iceland reported unmet dental care needs in 2024, compared to fewer than 1% in Germany, Hungary and the Netherlands, as well as accession country Croatia.

This varies considerably across OECD countries, from fewer than 2% of households experiencing catastrophic health spending in Sweden, Slovenia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands, to over 10% of households in Lithuania, Latvia and Hungary (Figure 5.10).
Data come mainly from administrative sources, although in some countries (including Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand and Switzerland) they come from health interview surveys.
Remote consultations cannot be distinguished and are included in a few countries (such as Austria from 2020, and Ireland, Japan, Latvia, the Netherlands, the Slovak Republic and Spain from 2019).

Figure 6.12 reveals broad consistency in the proportion of patients with diabetes on recommended antihypertensive medications in 2023, although Iceland, the Netherlands and Türkiye had rates at around 80% or lower.
At the other end of the scale, many of the Nordic countries, Canada and the Netherlands had a much lower proportion of spending on inpatient services – at around 20%.
By contrast, these shares were much lower in Norway, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, accounting for only one-tenth of health spending.
In countries with formal arrangements such as Norway, Sweden and the Netherlands, nearly 30% of all health spending was on long-term care services in 2023.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).
This compares with the Netherlands, Costa Rica, Mexico, Poland and the United Kingdom where dental care spending represents only around 3% of total health spending.
The latter provider group plays a much more central role in the health systems in the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland than elsewhere.
